```{=html}
<header class="dg-head dg-head-section"><p class="dg-kicker">Chapter 7 <span class="dg-sep">•</span> <a href="index.html">Metric</a></p><h1 class="dg-title"><span class="dg-secnum">7.1</span> Metric</h1></header>
<ul class="dg-itemize dg-depth-1">
<li><p>A <strong>metric</strong> <span class="math inline">\(g\)</span> on a smooth manifold <span class="math inline">\((\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}, \mathcal{A})\)</span> is a <span class="math inline">\((0,2)\)</span>-tensor field  <span class="math display">\begin{align*}
            g : \Gamma T\mathcal{M} \times \Gamma T\mathcal{M} &amp;\xlongrightarrow{\substack{\sim \\ \sim}} C^\infty(\mathcal{M}) \\
            (\mathcal{X}, \mathcal{Y})                         &amp;\longmapsto g(\mathcal{X}, \mathcal{Y}),
        \end{align*}</span>  satisfying the following two conditions:</p>
<ol class="dg-enumerate dg-depth-1">
<li><p><em>Symmetry:</em> <span class="math inline">\(g(\mathcal{X}, \mathcal{Y}) = g(\mathcal{Y}, \mathcal{X})\)</span> for all <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{X}, \mathcal{Y} \in \Gamma T\mathcal{M}\)</span>.</p></li>
<li><p><em>Invertibility of the musical map:</em> the <strong>musical map</strong>  <span class="math display">\begin{align*}
                    \flat : \Gamma T\mathcal{M} &amp;\longrightarrow \Gamma T^*\mathcal{M} \\
                    \mathcal{X} &amp;\longmapsto \flat(\mathcal{X}),
                    \qquad \text{with } \flat(\mathcal{X})\left\lceil \mathcal{Y} \right\rfloor \coloneqq g(\mathcal{X}, \mathcal{Y}),
                \end{align*}</span>  is an isomorphism of <span class="math inline">\(C^\infty(\mathcal{M})\)</span>-modules. Explicitly, <span class="math inline">\(\flat\)</span> must be</p>
<ol class="dg-enumerate dg-depth-2">
<li class="dg-labelled"><span class="dg-item-label">(a)</span> <p><span class="math inline">\(C^\infty(\mathcal{M})\)</span>-linear: <span class="math inline">\(\flat(f \, \mathcal{X} + \mathcal{Y}) = f \, \flat(\mathcal{X}) + \flat(\mathcal{Y})\)</span> for all <span class="math inline">\(f \in C^\infty(\mathcal{M})\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{X}, \mathcal{Y} \in \Gamma T\mathcal{M}\)</span>;</p></li>
<li class="dg-labelled"><span class="dg-item-label">(b)</span> <p>bijective: <span class="math inline">\(\forall \, \mathsf{X} \in \Gamma T^*\mathcal{M} \;\, \exists! \, \mathcal{X} \in \Gamma T\mathcal{M} : \flat(\mathcal{X}) = \mathsf{X}\)</span><sup class="dg-fnref"><a href="#fn-1" id="fnref-1" role="doc-noteref" aria-label="Footnote 1">1</a></sup>.</p></li>
</ol>
<p>That <span class="math inline">\(\flat(\mathcal{X})\)</span> is indeed a covector field, and condition (a) follow from the <span class="math inline">\(C^\infty(\mathcal{M})\)</span>-linearity of <span class="math inline">\(g\)</span> in its second and first slot, respectively. The actual requirement is (b).</p></li>
</ol>
<p>A <strong>metric manifold</strong> is the quadruple <span class="math inline">\((\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}, \mathcal{A}, g)\)</span>, i.e. a smooth manifold equipped with a metric.</p></li>
<li><p>In a chart <span class="math inline">\((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X})\)</span>, the <strong>components of the metric</strong> are the functions  <span class="math display">\[
            g_{ij} \coloneqq g(\partial x_i, \partial x_j) \in C^\infty(\mathcal{U}),
        \]</span>  with <span class="math inline">\(g_{ij} = g_{ji}\)</span> by symmetry. For <span class="math inline">\(\left. \mathcal{X} \right|_\mathcal{U} = x^i \, \partial x_i\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(\left. \mathcal{Y} \right|_\mathcal{U} = \tilde{x}^j \, \partial x_j\)</span>, <span class="math inline">\(C^\infty(\mathcal{M})\)</span>-bilinearity gives <span class="math inline">\(\left. g(\mathcal{X}, \mathcal{Y}) \right|_\mathcal{U} = x^i \, \tilde{x}^j \, g_{ij}\)</span>. When two charts are involved we write <span class="math inline">\((g_\mathscr{X})_{ij}\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\((g_\mathscr{Y})_{kl}\)</span>; as for any <span class="math inline">\((0,2)\)</span>-tensor field, on <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{U} \cap \mathcal{V}\)</span>,  <span class="math display">\[
            (g_\mathscr{Y})_{kl}
            = \frac{\partial \mathscr{X}^i}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^k} \,
            \frac{\partial \mathscr{X}^j}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^l}\,
            (g_\mathscr{X})_{ij}.
        \]</span></p></li>
<li><p>Since <span class="math inline">\(\flat\)</span> is an isomorphism, there exists the <strong>inverse musical map</strong>  <span class="math display">\begin{align*}
            \flat^{-1} : \Gamma T^*\mathcal{M} &amp;\longrightarrow \Gamma T\mathcal{M} \\
            \mathsf{X}                         &amp;\longmapsto \flat^{-1}(\mathsf{X}),
        \end{align*}</span>  which is <span class="math inline">\(C^\infty(\mathcal{M})\)</span>-linear as well (apply <span class="math inline">\(\flat^{-1}\)</span> to <span class="math inline">\(\flat\big( f \, \flat^{-1}(\mathsf{X}) + \flat^{-1}(\mathsf{Y}) \big) = f \, \mathsf{X} + \mathsf{Y}\)</span>). It defines the <strong>inverse metric</strong> <span class="math inline">\(g^{-1}\)</span>, the <span class="math inline">\((2,0)\)</span>-tensor field  <span class="math display">\begin{align*}
            g^{-1} : \Gamma T^*\mathcal{M} \times \Gamma T^*\mathcal{M} &amp;\xlongrightarrow{\substack{\sim \\ \sim}} C^\infty(\mathcal{M}) \\
            (\mathsf{X}, \mathsf{Y}) &amp;\longmapsto g^{-1}(\mathsf{X}, \mathsf{Y}) \coloneqq \mathsf{Y}\left\lceil \flat^{-1}(\mathsf{X}) \right\rfloor .
        \end{align*}</span>  It is symmetric: writing <span class="math inline">\(\mathsf{Y} = \flat\big( \flat^{-1}(\mathsf{Y}) \big)\)</span> and using the symmetry of <span class="math inline">\(g\)</span>,  <span class="math display">\[
            g^{-1}(\mathsf{X}, \mathsf{Y})
            = \flat\big( \flat^{-1}(\mathsf{Y}) \big)\left\lceil \flat^{-1}(\mathsf{X}) \right\rfloor
            = g\big( \flat^{-1}(\mathsf{Y}), \flat^{-1}(\mathsf{X}) \big)
            = g\big( \flat^{-1}(\mathsf{X}), \flat^{-1}(\mathsf{Y}) \big)
            = g^{-1}(\mathsf{Y}, \mathsf{X}),
        \]</span>  which also shows that <span class="math inline">\(g^{-1}\)</span> is simply <span class="math inline">\(g\)</span> evaluated on the vector fields corresponding to <span class="math inline">\(\mathsf{X}\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(\mathsf{Y}\)</span> under <span class="math inline">\(\flat^{-1}\)</span>. Its components in a chart are <span class="math inline">\((g^{-1})^{ij} \coloneqq g^{-1}(dx^i, dx^j) \in C^\infty(\mathcal{U})\)</span>.</p>
<p>In components, the inverse metric is characterized by <span class="math inline">\(g_{ij} \, (g^{-1})^{jk} = \delta_i^k\)</span><sup class="dg-fnref"><a href="#fn-2" id="fnref-2" role="doc-noteref" aria-label="Footnote 2">2</a></sup>. The matrix of components of <span class="math inline">\(g^{-1}\)</span> is the inverse of the matrix of components of <span class="math inline">\(g\)</span>.</p></li>
<li><p><em>Musical maps in components.</em> For <span class="math inline">\(\left. \mathcal{X} \right|_\mathcal{U} = x^j \, \partial x_j\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(\left. \mathsf{X} \right|_\mathcal{U} = \mathtt{x}_j \, dx^j\)</span>, the components of <span class="math inline">\(\flat(\mathcal{X}) \in \Gamma T^*\mathcal{M}\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(\flat^{-1}(\mathsf{X}) \in \Gamma T\mathcal{M}\)</span> are  <span class="math display">\begin{align*}
            \flat(\mathcal{X})_i
            &amp;\coloneqq \flat(\mathcal{X})\left\lceil \partial x_i \right\rfloor
            = g(x^i \partial x_i, \partial x_j)
            = x^j \, g_{ji},\\
            \flat^{-1}(\mathsf{X})^i
            &amp;\coloneqq dx^i\left\lceil \flat^{-1}(\mathsf{X}) \right\rfloor
            = g^{-1}(\mathtt{x}_j dx^j, dx^i)
            = \mathtt{x}_j \, (g^{-1})^{ji}.
        \end{align*}</span>  This is what is usually called “lowering” and “raising” indices with <span class="math inline">\(g\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(g^{-1}\)</span>. In these notes the results always keep their own names, <span class="math inline">\(\flat(\mathcal{X})_i\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(\flat^{-1}(\mathsf{X})^i\)</span>, and are never written as <span class="math inline">\(x_i\)</span> or <span class="math inline">\(\mathtt{x}^i\)</span>.</p></li>
</ul>
```

## `<span class="dg-secnum">7.1.1</span> Signature`{=html} {#subsection_Metric_Signature}

```{=html}
<ul class="dg-itemize dg-depth-1">
<li><p>Unlike a <span class="math inline">\((1,1)\)</span>-tensor field, <span class="math inline">\(g\)</span> has no eigenvalues. For a <span class="math inline">\((1,1)\)</span>-tensor <span class="math inline">\(T_p\)</span> at <span class="math inline">\(p\)</span>, the eigenvalue equation in components,  <span class="math display">\[
            T^i_j(p) \, x^j_p = \lambda \, x^i_p ,
        \]</span>  equates the components of two vectors, <span class="math inline">\(T_p(\cdot, \mathcal{X}_p)\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(\lambda \, \mathcal{X}_p\)</span>. It is thus the component form of a chart-independent equation, and <span class="math inline">\(\lambda\)</span> is the same in every chart. For the metric, the analogous equation  <span class="math display">\[
            g_{ij}(p) \, x^j_p = \lambda \, x^i_p
        \]</span>  equates the components of the covector <span class="math inline">\(\flat_p(\mathcal{X}_p)\)</span> with those of the vector <span class="math inline">\(\lambda \, \mathcal{X}_p\)</span>, which live in fundamentally different spaces. What survives is the so-called signature, as stated by <strong>Sylvester’s law of inertia</strong> (proved in Appendix <a class="dg-xref" href="../proofs-and-additional-material/proof-sylvester.html" data-kind="section" data-label="section_proof_Sylvester">B.12</a>): at every <span class="math inline">\(p \in \mathcal{M}\)</span> there exists a chart <span class="math inline">\((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X})\)</span> with <span class="math inline">\(p \in \mathcal{U}\)</span> whose components at <span class="math inline">\(p\)</span> are  <span class="math display">\[
            g_{ij}(p) = 0 \;\; \text{for } i \neq j,
            \qquad
            g_{ii}(p) \in \{+1, -1\},
        \]</span>  i.e. in which the chart-induced basis <span class="math inline">\(\{ (\partial x_1)_p, \dots, (\partial x_d)_p \}\)</span> of <span class="math inline">\(T_p\mathcal{M}\)</span> “diagonalizes” <span class="math inline">\(g_p\)</span>, and the number <span class="math inline">\(n_+\)</span> of <span class="math inline">\(+1\)</span>’s (and hence the number <span class="math inline">\(n_-\)</span> of <span class="math inline">\(-1\)</span>’s) does not depend on the chart chosen. No zeros appear because <span class="math inline">\(g_p\)</span> is non-degenerate<sup class="dg-fnref"><a href="#fn-3" id="fnref-3" role="doc-noteref" aria-label="Footnote 3">3</a></sup>, so <span class="math inline">\(n_+ + n_- = \dim(\mathcal{M})\)</span>. The doublet <span class="math inline">\((n_+, n_-)\)</span> is the <strong>signature</strong> of <span class="math inline">\(g\)</span> at <span class="math inline">\(p\)</span>. It is, in fact, the same at all points of a connected manifold<sup class="dg-fnref"><a href="#fn-4" id="fnref-4" role="doc-noteref" aria-label="Footnote 4">4</a></sup>, so we simply speak of the signature of <span class="math inline">\(g\)</span>. Metrics are classified according to it:</p>
<ol class="dg-enumerate dg-depth-1">
<li><p>If <span class="math inline">\(n_+ = \dim(\mathcal{M})\)</span>, the metric is <strong>Riemannian</strong>. It is then <strong>positive-definite</strong>,  <span class="math display">\[
                    g_p(\mathcal{X}_p, \mathcal{X}_p) &gt; 0 \qquad \forall \, \mathcal{X}_p \neq 0, \;\; \forall \, p \in \mathcal{M},
                \]</span>  so each <span class="math inline">\(g_p\)</span> is an <strong>inner product</strong> on <span class="math inline">\(T_p\mathcal{M}\)</span>. (If <span class="math inline">\(n_- = \dim(\mathcal{M})\)</span>, the metric is negative-definite and <span class="math inline">\(-g\)</span> is Riemannian; this case is conventionally included.)</p></li>
<li><p>If <span class="math inline">\(0 &lt; n_+ &lt; \dim(\mathcal{M})\)</span>, the metric is <strong>pseudo-Riemannian</strong>. Then there exist non-zero <strong>null vectors</strong>, <span class="math inline">\(g_p(\mathcal{X}_p, \mathcal{X}_p) = 0\)</span> with <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{X}_p \neq 0\)</span>: if <span class="math inline">\(g_{aa}(p) = +1\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(g_{bb}(p) = -1\)</span> in such a chart, take <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{X}_p = (\partial x_a)_p + (\partial x_b)_p\)</span>. Each <span class="math inline">\(g_p\)</span> is thus symmetric, bilinear and non-degenerate, but not positive-definite: a <strong>pseudo-inner product</strong>. In the special case <span class="math inline">\(n_+ = 1\)</span> or <span class="math inline">\(n_- = 1\)</span> (with <span class="math inline">\(\dim(\mathcal{M}) \geq 2\)</span>) the metric is <strong>Lorentzian</strong>; both sign conventions, <span class="math inline">\((1, d-1)\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\((d-1, 1)\)</span>, are common in the literature.</p></li>
</ol></li>
</ul>
<section class="dg-footnotes" role="doc-endnotes"><div class="dg-fn" id="fn-1" role="doc-footnote"><a class="dg-fn-num" href="#fnref-1" aria-label="Back to the text">1</a><div class="dg-fn-body"><p>This can be checked pointwise. At each <span class="math inline">\(p\)</span>, <span class="math inline">\(\flat_p : T_p\mathcal{M} \to T_p^*\mathcal{M}\)</span>, <span class="math inline">\(\flat_p(\mathcal{X}_p)(\mathcal{Y}_p) \coloneqq g_p(\mathcal{X}_p, \mathcal{Y}_p)\)</span>, with <span class="math inline">\(\flat(\mathcal{X})_p = \flat_p(\mathcal{X}_p)\)</span>. Since <span class="math inline">\(\dim T_p\mathcal{M} = \dim T_p^*\mathcal{M}\)</span>, (b) <span class="math inline">\(\iff\)</span> (i) <span class="math inline">\(\flat_p\)</span> is an isomorphism <span class="math inline">\(\forall \, p\)</span> <span class="math inline">\(\iff\)</span> (ii) <span class="math inline">\(\ker \flat_p = \{0\} \;\, \forall \, p\)</span>, i.e. <span class="math inline">\(g\)</span> is <strong>non-degenerate</strong>: <span class="math inline">\(g_p(\mathcal{X}_p, \mathcal{Y}_p) = 0 \;\, \forall \, \mathcal{Y}_p \Rightarrow \mathcal{X}_p = 0\)</span> <span class="math inline">\(\iff\)</span> (iii) <span class="math inline">\(\det\big( g_{ij}(p) \big) \neq 0 \;\, \forall \, p\)</span>, in every chart. (i) <span class="math inline">\(\Rightarrow\)</span> (b): <span class="math inline">\(\flat^{-1}(\mathsf{X})_p \coloneqq \flat_p^{-1}(\mathsf{X}_p)\)</span> is smooth, its components being <span class="math inline">\(\mathtt{x}_j\)</span> times the entries of <span class="math inline">\(\big( g_{ij} \big)^{-1}\)</span>. (b) <span class="math inline">\(\Rightarrow\)</span> (i): if <span class="math inline">\(\flat_{p_0}\)</span> were singular, any <span class="math inline">\(\mathsf{Y}\)</span> with <span class="math inline">\(\mathsf{Y}_{p_0} \notin \operatorname{im} \flat_{p_0}\)</span> (constant components near <span class="math inline">\(p_0\)</span> times a bump function) would have no preimage, as <span class="math inline">\(\flat(\mathcal{X})_{p_0} = \flat_{p_0}(\mathcal{X}_{p_0})\)</span>. Strictly weaker is injectivity alone, <span class="math inline">\(g(\mathcal{X}, \mathcal{Y}) = 0 \;\, \forall \, \mathcal{Y} \Rightarrow \mathcal{X} = 0\)</span>: <span class="math inline">\(g = (\mathscr{X}^1)^2 \, dx^1 \otimes dx^1\)</span> on <span class="math inline">\(\mathbb{R}\)</span> satisfies it, yet <span class="math inline">\(g_0 = 0\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(dx^1 \notin \operatorname{im} \flat\)</span>, since <span class="math inline">\(\flat(x \, \partial x_1) = (\mathscr{X}^1)^2 \, x \, dx^1 = dx^1\)</span> requires <span class="math inline">\(x = (\mathscr{X}^1)^{-2}\)</span>, not smooth at <span class="math inline">\(0\)</span>.</p></div></div><div class="dg-fn" id="fn-2" role="doc-footnote"><a class="dg-fn-num" href="#fnref-2" aria-label="Back to the text">2</a><div class="dg-fn-body"><p>The name “inverse” does not mean that <span class="math inline">\(g^{-1}\)</span> is the inverse of <span class="math inline">\(g\)</span> as a map: <span class="math inline">\(g\)</span> is a map from pairs of vector fields to scalar fields, so it has no inverse in that sense. It refers instead to the relation between the matrices of components, which follows from <span class="math inline">\(\flat^{-1}\)</span> being the inverse of <span class="math inline">\(\flat\)</span>. Since <span class="math inline">\(\flat(\partial x_k)\left\lceil \partial x_l \right\rfloor = g_{kl}\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(dx^k\left\lceil \flat^{-1}(dx^j) \right\rfloor = (g^{-1})^{jk}\)</span>, we have <span class="math inline">\(\flat(\partial x_k) = g_{kl} \, dx^l\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(\flat^{-1}(dx^j) = (g^{-1})^{jk} \, \partial x_k\)</span>. Hence <span class="math inline">\(\partial x_i = \flat^{-1}\big( \flat(\partial x_i) \big) = g_{ij} \, (g^{-1})^{jk} \, \partial x_k\)</span>, and similarly <span class="math inline">\(dx^j = \flat\big( \flat^{-1}(dx^j) \big) = (g^{-1})^{jk} \, g_{kl} \, dx^l\)</span>, which, the chart-induced frames being bases, give <span class="math inline">\(g_{ij} \, (g^{-1})^{jk} = \delta_i{}^k\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\((g^{-1})^{jk} \, g_{kl} = \delta^j{}_l\)</span>.</p></div></div><div class="dg-fn" id="fn-3" role="doc-footnote"><a class="dg-fn-num" href="#fnref-3" aria-label="Back to the text">3</a><div class="dg-fn-body"><p>Sylvester’s law holds for any symmetric bilinear form on <span class="math inline">\(T_p\mathcal{M}\)</span>, degenerate or not: in a suitable basis it is diagonal with entries in <span class="math inline">\(\{+1, -1, 0\}\)</span>, and the numbers <span class="math inline">\((n_+, n_-, n_0)\)</span> of each do not depend on the basis, with <span class="math inline">\(n_0 = \dim \ker \flat_p\)</span>. For a metric, <span class="math inline">\(\flat_p\)</span> is an isomorphism, so <span class="math inline">\(n_0 = 0\)</span>. Appendix <a class="dg-xref" href="../proofs-and-additional-material/proof-sylvester.html" data-kind="section" data-label="section_proof_Sylvester">B.12</a> proves only the non-degenerate case.</p></div></div><div class="dg-fn" id="fn-4" role="doc-footnote"><a class="dg-fn-num" href="#fnref-4" aria-label="Back to the text">4</a><div class="dg-fn-body"><p>In a chart, the eigenvalues of the symmetric matrix <span class="math inline">\(\big( g_{ij}(p) \big)\)</span> must depend continuously on <span class="math inline">\(p\)</span>. Since their product, <span class="math inline">\(\det\big( g_{ij}(p) \big)\)</span>, never vanishes, no eigenvalue can change sign, so the signature is locally constant, hence constant on a connected manifold.</p></div></div></section>
```
